usage: use 켜다/끄다 (on/off) like any appliance; 틀다 also works for 'crank it on'
고장 나다 is the set phrase for any machine failing; 나다 makes it intransitive
a real button (외출 = going out) that keeps pipes from freezing while saving gas
돌리다 (lit. 'make it spin/turn') is the idiomatic 'run an appliance' verb here
examples: 보일러를 켜요.
I turn on the boiler.
simple present; 켜다 = switch on, the most basic pairing
겨울인데 보일러가 안 돼서 너무 추워요.
It's winter and the boiler isn't working, so it's freezing.
안 되다 = 'not function'; ~아서 links cause to result
집주인한테 보일러 좀 고쳐 달라고 연락했어요.
I contacted the landlord asking them to please fix the boiler.
real tenant move: ~한테 (to a person) + ~아 달라고 하다 (request a favor)
nuance: 보일러 is a katakana-route loanword (from English 'boiler') but in a Korean home it means far more than the English word: one 보일러 heats BOTH the 온돌 floor and the hot-water supply, so when it dies you lose heat and hot showers at the same moment. Do not confuse it with 난방 (the heating itself, the warmth) or 히터 (a plug-in space heater) — 보일러 is the gas unit that produces 난방. The habitual verbs are 켜다/끄다 (on/off), 틀다 ('crank on'), and 돌리다 ('run it'), while a breakdown is always 고장 나다. The classic English-speaker pitfall is saying 보일러가 죽었어요 ('the boiler died') as a direct translation of an English idiom; Koreans say 보일러가 고장 났어요 or 보일러가 안 돼요. Tenants report a dead 보일러 to the 집주인 (landlord) or 관리사무소 (management office) immediately, since no hot water is an emergency.

mistakes: English speakers say 보일러가 죽었어요 ('the boiler died'), copying an English idiom. Machines in Korean do not 'die'; the correct phrase is 보일러가 고장 났어요 or 보일러가 안 돼요.
Saying 보일러를 열다 ('open the boiler') by translating 'turn on' loosely is wrong; 열다 is for doors/lids. Appliances take 켜다 (or 틀다/돌리다), so it's 보일러를 켜다.
Mixing up 보일러 with 난방: 난방이 고장 났어요 sounds odd because 난방 is the abstract heating. The physical unit that broke is the 보일러, so 보일러가 고장 났어요 is what a repair person expects.

usage: 생기다 = 'come into being'; the neutral verb for a problem showing up
발생하다 (occur) is the formal register you use when filing a 관리사무소 report
신고 = official report; 누수 신고를 하다 = lodge a leak complaint with management
흔적 = mark left behind (a water stain on the ceiling proving past leakage)
examples: 천장에서 물이 새요.
Water is leaking from the ceiling.
casual everyday phrasing: the verb 새다 (to leak), not the noun
천장에서 물이 떨어져서 누수인 것 같아요.
Water is dripping from the ceiling, so I think it's a leak.
~인 것 같다 = 'seems to be ~', a soft diagnosis
윗집에서 누수가 생겨서 집주인한테 연락했어요.
There's a leak from the upstairs unit, so I called the landlord.
누수가 생기다 = a leak occurs; 집주인한테 연락하다 = contact the landlord
nuance: 누수 is Sino-Korean: 漏水, literally 漏 'leak/seep' + 水 'water', i.e. 'leaking water'. Because it is a 한자어 noun it carries a formal, technical tone — it is the word you use when reporting damage to a 관리사무소, 집주인, or repair technician, and it appears on invoices and insurance forms. The dividing line you must learn: 누수 is a NOUN naming the phenomenon, whereas the everyday verb 'to leak' is 새다 (물이 새요). So a native speaker casually says 물이 새요 but writes 누수가 발생했습니다 on a report. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating 누수 like a verb and producing 누수해요 — this does not exist; you must say 물이 새요 or 누수가 생겼어요. Also distinguish 누수 (water leaking) from its dangerous lookalike 누전 (漏電, electrical leakage/short circuit), and from 결로 (condensation), which looks like a leak but is just humidity beading on a cold surface. Establishing the source — 윗집 (upstairs) vs. building pipes — decides who pays.

usage: the idiomatic verb: mold 'blossoms' like a flower — present 피어요, past 폈어요
슬다 is the native verb for mold/rust forming on a surface; common in speech
제거하다 (formal 'eliminate'); casually 곰팡이를 닦다 (wipe off) or 없애다
냄새 = smell; 곰팡이 냄새가 나다 = it smells musty, a tell-tale of hidden mold
examples: 벽에 곰팡이가 많아요.
There's a lot of mold on the wall.
location marked by 에; the simplest description
장마철에는 욕실에 곰팡이가 잘 피어요.
During the rainy season, mold easily grows in the bathroom.
잘 + verb = 'easily/often'; 피어요 is from 피다 (to bloom), the verb mold takes
곰팡이 때문에 벽지를 다 뜯어내고 새로 도배했어요.
Because of the mold, I tore out all the wallpaper and re-papered.
real consequence; ~때문에 (because of) + 뜯어내다 (rip out)
nuance: 곰팡이 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) for mold/mildew, and it is a constant battle in Korean homes — in humid 욕실 (bathrooms), behind furniture pushed against cold exterior walls, and all through 장마 (the summer rainy season). The crucial collocation is the verb: mold 곰팡이가 피다, literally 'mold blooms', as if it were a flower (present 곰팡이가 피어요, past 곰팡이가 폈어요). A second native verb, 슬다 (곰팡이가 슬다 'mold sets in'), is also fully natural. The sharp pitfall for learners is the verb pair 피다 vs. 펴다: 피다 ('to bloom', intransitive) is what mold does, while 펴다 ('to unfold/spread out', transitive — you 펴 a blanket or an umbrella) is a different verb; never say 곰팡이를 펴다. Another mistake is translating 'mold grows' as 곰팡이가 자라요 — 자라다 is for living things like children or plants, so for mold Koreans say 폈어요 or 슬었어요. Do not confuse 곰팡이 with 먼지 (dust) or 때 (grime). Serious 곰팡이 is legitimate grounds to ask a 집주인 for repairs.

usage: 환기 + 하다 = the everyday verb: open the windows and let air through
시키다 (causative 'make it happen') — 환기를 시키다 stresses you actively cause airflow
잘 되다 = 'works well'; 환기가 잘 돼요 praises a room's airflow
for a cross-breeze to blow through
맞바람 = cross-draft; opening windows on two sides so 맞바람이 쳐서 환기가 잘 돼요
examples: 환기를 해요.
I air out the room.
환기 + 하다, the most basic form
곰팡이가 안 생기게 매일 환기를 시켜요.
I air it out every day so mold doesn't form.
~게 (so that) + causative 시키다; ties ventilation to mold prevention
이 방은 창문이 작아서 환기가 잘 안 돼요.
This room has a small window, so it doesn't ventilate well.
real flaw to flag when viewing a place; 잘 안 되다 = 'doesn't work well'
nuance: 환기 is Sino-Korean: 換氣, literally 換 'change/exchange' + 氣 'air', i.e. 'changing out the air'. Koreans treat daily 환기 as serious housekeeping, because tightly sealed, well-insulated apartments trap cooking smells, CO2, and the moisture that breeds 곰팡이; you 환기 after cooking, after sleeping, and especially on dry winter days. The word takes BOTH 하다 and 시키다 — 환기하다 and 환기시키다 — and here they are effectively interchangeable, both meaning 'open up and let air through'; 시키다 just foregrounds that you are deliberately causing it. Distinguish 환기 sharply from 통풍 (通風), which is the passive property of air being able to pass through a space (a breezy room has good 통풍), whereas 환기 is the active act of refreshing the air. Also keep it apart from 난방 (heating) and 냉방 (cooling) — those change temperature, 환기 changes the air itself. The English-speaker pitfall: 환기 is a noun, so do not bolt it onto random verbs; pair it only with 하다/시키다, or describe airflow with 환기가 잘 되다/안 되다.

usage: 내다 = pay (a fee/bill); the standard verb for any 공과금
나오다 (lit. 'comes out') is how Koreans say a bill is issued/lands
포함되다 = be included; the make-or-break rental question 'is it 포함이에요?'
요금 (料金, fee) is the technically correct word; on bills you see 상수도 요금
examples: 수도세를 내요.
I pay the water bill.
object marker 를 + 내다, the core pairing
월세에 수도세가 포함되어 있어요?
Is the water bill included in the monthly rent?
the essential question before signing; 포함되어 있다 = is included
누수 때문에 수도세 폭탄을 맞았어요.
I got hit with a huge water bill because of a leak.
real shock: 요금 폭탄을 맞다 = 'get hit by a bill bomb'
nuance: 수도세 is one of the 공과금 (utility bills) tenants juggle, and it sits in a funny spot: it ends in 세 (稅, 'tax'), but a water charge is really a usage fee, so the textbook-correct term is 수도 요금 (水道料金) — 水道 'water-way/plumbing' + 料金 'fee'. In daily life, though, everyone says 수도세, just as they say 전기세 and 가스비. The verbs are register-defining: a bill 나오다 ('comes out', is issued) and you 내다 (pay) it — never 사다 (buy). The make-or-break rental question is whether it's 포함 (included) in the rent or paid separately. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers: first, do not buy a bill — 'pay the bill' is 수도세를 내다, and 'the bill was high' is 수도세가 많이 나왔어요, literally 'a lot came out'. Second, do not confuse 수도세 (the monetary bill) with 수돗물 (tap water, the actual H2O) — note the sai-siot ㅅ in 수돗물. The slang 요금 폭탄 ('bill bomb') describes a shockingly high bill, often traced to a hidden 누수.

usage: 내다 = pay; the standard verb across all utility bills
나오다 = is issued; 많이 나오다 = comes out high
폭탄 (爆彈, bomb) = a shockingly high bill, the classic summer-AC complaint
요금 (料金, fee) is the accurate term; you see 전기 요금 on official KEPCO bills
examples: 전기세를 내요.
I pay the electricity bill.
를 + 내다, the base pattern
에어컨을 많이 틀어서 전기세가 무서워요.
I ran the AC a lot, so I'm scared of the electricity bill.
틀다 = crank on (an appliance); 무섭다 here = 'dreadful to think about'
전기세가 지난달보다 두 배나 나왔어요.
The electricity bill came out double last month's.
comparison with 보다 (than) + 나/emphasis ('a whopping two times')
nuance: 전기세 follows the same 세 (稅 'tax') vs. 요금 (料金 'fee') split as 수도세: the formally correct term is 전기 요금 (電氣料金), 電氣 'electricity' + 料金 'fee', because it is a usage charge, not a tax — yet 전기세 is what everyone actually says. What makes 전기세 special is Korea's 누진제 (累進制, progressive rate system): residential electricity is billed in escalating tiers, so heavy summer 에어컨 use can push you into a high bracket and spike the bill dramatically, which is why 전기세 폭탄 ('electricity bill bomb') is a fixed summer complaint. Verbs follow the bill pattern: it 나오다 (comes out/is issued) and you 내다 (pay) it. The pitfalls: first, do not confuse 전기세 (the bill, the money owed) with 전기 (電氣) itself, the electricity — 전기가 나갔어요 means 'the power went out', a totally different sentence from 전기세가 많이 나왔어요. Second, resist English 'high bill' as 전기세가 높아요; the idiom is 전기세가 많이 나왔어요. Unplugging unused 콘센트 (outlets) is the stereotypical 전기세-saving habit.

usage: 내다 = pay; note this one ends in 비 (費, expense), not 세
나오다 = is issued; 겨울에 많이 나오다 = comes out high in winter
the gas bill is a burden
부담되다 = to weigh on you financially; a natural way to say a cost stings
도시가스 (都市gas, piped city gas) + 요금; the official term on the bill
examples: 가스비를 내요.
I pay the gas bill.
를 + 내다, the core pattern
가스비 아끼려고 보일러를 외출 모드로 해 놔요.
To save on gas, I keep the boiler on away mode.
~려고 (in order to) + 해 놓다 (do and leave it that way) — a money-saving habit
이번 겨울은 가스비가 작년보다 더 비싸게 나왔어요.
This winter the gas bill came out more expensive than last year.
real comparison; 보다 (than) + 비싸게 나오다
nuance: 가스비 is worth noticing for one detail: unlike 전기세 and 수도세, it conventionally ends in 비 (費, 'expense/cost'), not 세 (稅, 'tax') — so the form is 가스비, and the fully formal term is 도시가스 요금 (都市가스料金, 'city-gas charge'). usage: 도배 + 하다 = the verb 'to do wallpapering'; the noun alone is not a verb
새로 = anew; the standard phrase for refreshing walls before move-in
비용 (費用, expense); a key negotiation figure with a landlord
the fixed pair Koreans name together when assessing or renovating a rental
examples: 도배를 새로 했어요.
I had it freshly wallpapered.
새로 하다 = redo from new; the most common everyday use
곰팡이 때문에 도배를 다시 해야 해요.

Korea papers walls rather than painting them as the default finish, so 도배 is a routine event whenever someone moves in or prepares a unit to rent, and it is almost always spoken of as a pair with 장판 (the vinyl flooring): 도배랑 장판 새로 해 주세요 is a stock request to a 집주인. usage: 깔다 (to spread/lay down flat) is THE verb for flooring, mats, blankets
들뜨다 = to come unstuck and bulge; the most common 장판 defect
누렇다 (deep yellow) describes aged vinyl; grounds to ask for new 장판
the standard rental-checklist pair, named together for move-in renovation
examples: 장판이 깨끗해요.
The floor covering is clean.
simple description of condition with 깨끗하다
보일러를 켜면 장판이 따뜻해져요.
When I turn on the boiler, the floor covering gets warm.
~면 (when/if) + 따뜻해지다 (become warm); the 온돌 effect on the vinyl
오래된 장판이 누래서 새로 깔았어요.

The signature collocation is the verb 깔다 ('to spread/lay flat'): you 장판을 깔다, the same verb you use to lay a mat or 이불 (bedding). Keep 장판 distinct from 바닥 (the floor structure itself, the ground you stand on) — 장판 is the covering ON the 바닥 — and from 마루 (wood-plank/parquet flooring) and 타일 (tile); 장판 specifically means the soft vinyl sheet. Like 도배, it is a fixed item on the rental checklist and is almost always paired with it: 도배랑 장판. Defects have set vocabulary worth knowing: 장판이 들뜨다 (lifts/bubbles up), 장판이 누렇다 (has yellowed with age), and water damage from 누수 soaking 장판 밑 (under the flooring). usage: 꽂다 (to insert/stick in) is the verb for putting a plug in
뽑다 (to pull out) is the opposite of 꽂다; the 전기세-saving move
부족하다 = to be insufficient; a stock complaint about older/small rooms
멀티탭 (multi-tap) extends one 콘센트 into many; what you buy when outlets are scarce
examples: 콘센트가 어디에 있어요?
Where is the outlet?
asking location with 어디에 (at where); a daily-life question
휴대폰 충전기를 콘센트에 꽂았어요.
I plugged the phone charger into the outlet.
에 꽂다 = plug INTO; the destination-marking 에
외출할 때 안 쓰는 콘센트는 다 뽑아 놔요.

~ㄹ 때 (when) + 뽑아 놓다 (unplug and leave it); a saving habit
nuance: 콘센트 is a sneaky loanword: it comes via Japanese コンセント, itself a clipping of English 'concentric plug', so despite the spelling it has NOTHING to do with English 'consent' — it simply means the wall socket. You must keep three pieces separate: the 콘센트 is the socket in the wall; the 플러그 (plug) is on the end of the appliance cord; and the verbs are 꽂다 (to plug in/insert) and 뽑다 (to pull out/unplug). So 충전기를 콘센트에 꽂다 = 'plug the charger into the outlet'. The number of 콘센트 is a genuine concern in older or small Korean rooms, and the fix is a 멀티탭 (power strip, 'multi-tap'), another Konglish term. Unplugging idle devices at the 콘센트 is the classic 전기세-saving habit. Pitfalls for English speakers: first, never read 콘센트 as 'consent' — it is purely the outlet. Second, do not blur 콘센트 (the wall socket) with 플러그 (the cord's plug); 'plug it in' targets the 콘센트 (꽂다), while the thing you hold is the 플러그. Third, mind the verbs — you 꽂다/뽑다 a plug, you do not '열다/닫다' (open/close) an outlet.

usage: 버리다 = to discard; the core verb, but it must go in the right bin
분리하다 (分離, to separate) from 일반쓰레기 and 재활용; legally required
봉투 = bag; you buy the official 음식물 전용 봉투 to dispose of it
냄새가 나다 = it stinks; the summer problem that forces frequent disposal
examples: 음식물쓰레기를 버려요.
I throw out the food waste.
를 + 버리다, the base pattern
음식물쓰레기는 일반 쓰레기랑 따로 버려야 해요.
Food waste has to be thrown out separately from regular trash.
the key residency rule; ~랑 따로 (apart from) + ~아야 하다 (must)
우리 아파트는 음식물쓰레기를 카드로 버려요.
Our apartment disposes of food waste by card.
real system: RFID smart bins; 카드로 (by card) marks the means
nuance: 음식물쓰레기 is a transparent compound: 음식물 (飮食物, 'food/edibles') + 쓰레기 (native word for 'trash') — so literally 'food trash'. The thing every newcomer must internalize is that Korean law mandates separating garbage into at least three streams: 음식물쓰레기 (food waste), 일반쓰레기 (general non-recyclable trash), and 재활용 (recycling). 음식물쓰레기 goes only into designated bins — often weight-based RFID units in apartments where you tag a 카드 and dump it, or into official 음식물 전용 봉투 (yellow food-waste bags) elsewhere. Getting it wrong can mean a 과태료 (administrative fine) or an irritated 관리사무소, so it is a real survival skill. The verbs: you 버리다 (throw out) it and you 분리하다 / 분리수거하다 (sort it out for collection). Pitfalls: first, do not lump it with general trash — 음식물쓰레기 vs. 일반쓰레기 is a legal line, not a preference. Second, note what does NOT count as 음식물쓰레기 even though it came from food: large bones, eggshells, shellfish/clam shells, onion skins, and tea bags are 일반쓰레기, because the rule is roughly 'can livestock eat it?'. Getting that boundary wrong is the most common foreigner mistake.

usage: 내다 = pay; charged monthly on top of 월세
나오다 = is issued/billed; 많이 나오다 = comes out high
to be included in the maintenance fee
포함되다 = be included; ask what the 관리비 covers before signing
별도 (別途, separate) = not included in the advertised rent; a listing red flag
examples: 관리비를 내요.
I pay the maintenance fee.
를 + 내다, the base pattern
관리비에 수도세랑 청소비가 포함되어 있어요.
The maintenance fee includes the water bill and cleaning fee.
what it covers; 포함되어 있다 = is included
겨울에는 난방비 때문에 관리비가 확 올라가요.
In winter the maintenance fee jumps because of heating costs.
real seasonal spike; 확 (sharply, all at once) + 올라가다 (go up)
nuance: 관리비 is Sino-Korean: 管理費, literally 管理 'management' + 費 'expense', i.e. 'management/maintenance fee'. It is the monthly building-upkeep charge covering shared costs — cleaning, security (경비), the elevator (엘리베이터), corridor lighting, and very often part of the utilities (수도세, 난방비, sometimes 인터넷) — and crucially it is billed ON TOP OF 월세 (monthly rent), which blindsides many newcomers. Always ask what the 관리비 covers and whether it's 포함 (included) or 별도 (別途, 'separate'), because a temptingly cheap 월세 can hide a fat 관리비. Like other recurring charges it 나오다 (comes out) and you 내다 (pay) it. Pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not confuse 관리비 (the monthly, non-refundable maintenance fee) with 보증금 (保證金, the large refundable deposit you get back when you leave) — they are completely different money. Second, do not assume rent already includes it the way some Western 'all-bills-included' rents do; in Korea 관리비 is usually a separate line. Third, distinguish 관리비 (shared building costs) from the individually-metered 공과금 like personal 전기세 — though some 관리비 bills bundle a portion of utilities, so reading the 관리비 고지서 (statement) itemization matters.
